PMGT1711 Week 01

PMGT1711 Week 01 - Why Systems Thinking Matters in Projects

Overview

Projects do not deliver isolated objects; they intervene in webs of interacting parts. This week introduces systems thinking for projects:

• What a system is: interacting parts, not merely a pile of components.

• Three complementary project perspectives: asset, system and conversation.

• Nested systems: a team inside a project inside a program and organisation, all inside a wider socio-cultural context.

• How systems thinking developed historically, and what a complex adaptive system is.

• Distinguishing clear (simple), complicated, complex and chaotic system contexts, and the response pattern suited to each.

• Types of project complexity, and how to think about risk and uncertainty, from known knowns to Black Swan events.

Key Concepts

What a system is

A system is a set of interacting or interrelated parts whose interactions produce the behaviour of the whole. It is not just a set (collection) of parts. The parts matter through the relationships between them: analysing each component in isolation misses the system's behaviour, which emerges from the interactions.

Example: a box of unassembled flat-pack furniture contains all the parts, but there are no functional relationships between them yet, so it is not a working system. Once assembled, the parts interact (the frame supports the seat, the screws hold the joints) and the object functions as a system.

Three complementary project perspectives

Every project can be viewed through three lenses, and a complex project needs all three at once (they coexist; one does not replace another in a sequence):

• Asset perspective: the characteristics and specifications of the deliverable itself, what is being built and how it is specified.

• System perspective: the wider operational environment in which the asset will function, plus the delivery system - the people, organisations and resources that carry the project through concept, design, construction and operation.

• Conversation perspective: the ongoing dialogue among stakeholders that surfaces their interests and their emotional and rational responses, and that builds the alignment needed for people to act.

Nested systems

Systems sit inside larger systems. A team is nested in a project, which is nested in a program, a portfolio and an organisation, which are in turn embedded in a broader socio-cultural context. Decisions at one level constrain and are constrained by the levels around it, so a project cannot be understood in isolation from its surrounding systems.

Historical roots of systems thinking

Modern systems thinking grew out of a sequence of intellectual moves:

Enlightenment-era reductionist (mechanistic) thinking: explain a whole by breaking it into parts and studying each part.

Organismic and holistic biology: living wholes cannot be fully explained by their parts, because the organisation of the parts matters.

General systems theory and cybernetics (the study of communication and control in systems), followed by complexity approaches.

Building on this, a complex adaptive system (CAS) is a system of agents that learn and adapt their behaviour as they interact, so the system's outcomes are emergent (produced by the interactions, not designed in advance). Emergence alone is not a complete definition of a CAS; the presence of learning, adapting agents is essential.

Risk and uncertainty

Uncertainty comes in several forms:

• Known knowns: facts you are aware of and can plan around.

• Known unknowns: recognised gaps in your knowledge, which can be managed (for example with contingency or further investigation).

• Unknown unknowns: surprises you did not foresee at all.

• Unknown knowns: things you should have known but did not, for example knowledge that exists somewhere in the organisation but never reaches the decision-makers.

A Black Swan event is an outcome outside regular expectations: it is extreme in impact, and after the fact people rationalise it as predictable in hindsight. Because classification depends on the observer's prior knowledge, not every surprise qualifies as a Black Swan.

Frameworks and Formulas

System contexts and response patterns

The nature of a system's interactions and uncertainty determines which kind of context you are in and therefore how you should act. Size alone does not distinguish them: a complicated problem has causal chains that can be discovered with expertise, while a complex one has interacting, adapting agents whose outcomes are emergent.

Context

Characteristics

Response pattern

Clear (simple)

Stable, cause-and-effect relationships are obvious to everyone

Sense - categorise - respond: identify the situation, place it in a known category, apply the standard response

Complicated

Cause-and-effect chains exist but are not obvious; expertise and analysis are needed to find them

Sense - analyse - respond: identify the situation, investigate the causal chains, then act

Complex

Interacting agents adapt to one another; outcomes are emergent and only visible after the fact

Probe - sense - respond: run small safe-to-fail experiments, learn from the results, then act

Chaotic

Cause-and-effect relationships cannot be established in time; the situation is unstable and demands immediate action

Act - sense - respond: act to stabilise, observe the effect, then move the situation to another context

Worked Examples

Flat-pack furniture: a set is not a system

A box of unassembled flat-pack furniture has every component of the final product, yet it cannot be used as a table or chair. The components are present, but the functional relationships that would make them support one another are missing. Assembling the furniture creates the interactions; only then does the collection of parts behave as a system. The lesson: a system is defined by its interacting parts, not by the presence of the parts alone.

WestConnex: one project seen through three lenses

WestConnex, a motorway project in Sydney, shows why all three project perspectives are needed together:

• Asset: the physical road itself, with its engineering specifications.

• System: the road sits inside Sydney's wider transport network and is produced by a network of delivering organisations, spanning concept, design, construction and operation.

• Conversation: continuous political, community and stakeholder dialogue about the project's effects and priorities.

Treating the project as only the road (asset) would miss both its operational setting (system) and the alignment work among stakeholders (conversation); complex projects require all three.

Pesticide case: a hidden causal chain

A farmer sprayed pesticide to kill one insect pest. After that insect disappeared, a second pest - previously kept in check by the first - exploded in population and damaged the crop. The situation is classified as complicated, not clear: there is a real, discoverable causal chain (removing one species removes the control on another species, which then harms the crop), but the chain is hidden and not obvious at first sight. In a clear context the cause-and-effect link would be immediately visible to everyone, which is not the case here.
